tip: To report an order, use 'dire di' plus the infinitive: 'digli di venire' = tell him to come.
When a pronoun attaches to 'di'', the 'tu' command of 'dire', its consonant doubles: 'di'' plus 'mi' becomes 'dimmi'.
A reflexive 'tu' command attaches the pronoun to the end of the verb: 'alzati' = get yourself up.
'Ci' can mean there, standing in for a place already mentioned: 'ci torno' = I go back there.
In proverbs 'chi' means whoever or the one who: 'chi cerca trova' = whoever searches finds.
Before another object pronoun, 'mi' changes to 'me': 'me lo dai' = will you give it to me.
'Recitare' usually means to act or perform on stage, not to recite: 'lei recita a teatro'.
'Casa' drops the article in the fixed phrase 'a casa', meaning home: 'vi porto a casa'.
'Le' is the indirect pronoun for to her: 'le scrivo una email' = I write an email to her.
A past participle agrees with 'lo' or 'la' before it: 'l'ho visto' for masculine, 'l'ho vista' for feminine.
'Ne' replaces of them, and 'ci' becomes 'ce' in front of it: 'ce ne sono molti' = there are many of them.
'Quello che' means what in the sense of the thing that: 'faccio quello che posso' = I do what I can.
A formal command with 'Lei' uses 'parli' instead of 'parla': 'parli più forte' = speak louder.
Possessives normally keep the article: 'la mia famiglia', not just 'mia famiglia'.
'Dei' works as some here, 'di' plus 'i' fused: 'dei fiori' = some flowers.
'Non' paired with 'più' means no more or not anymore: 'non ce ne sono più' = there are none left.
'Il quale' (or 'la quale') is a formal alternative to 'che': 'il quale è molto importante' = which is very important.
'L'anno scorso' marks a finished past point, so it pairs with the 'passato prossimo': 'sono stato l'anno scorso'.
For the time when something happens, use 'in cui': 'l'anno in cui sono nato' = the year when I was born.
Weather often uses the verb 'fare': 'fa caldo' means it is hot, literally it makes heat.
'Al posto di' someone means in their shoes or situation: 'al mio posto' = in my place.
'Dammelo' is 'da'' + 'me' + 'lo' (give me it); after the short command 'da'' the pronoun's consonant doubles, hence the double m.
For a completed action after 'spero che', use the past subjunctive 'abbia' plus the participle: 'abbia fatto'.
'Valere la pena' means to be worth it: 'valga la pena provare' = it is worth trying.
Italian has fear rather than being afraid: 'avere paura', so 'abbia paura' = you are afraid.
'Che' covers both who and that when pointing back to a person or thing: 'l'uomo che ho incontrato' = the man that I met.
'Da' questo libro' uses the short 'tu' command: 'da'', 'di'', 'fa'', 'va'', 'sta'' all cut to one syllable, the apostrophe marking the drop.
'Purché', meaning as long as, always takes the subjunctive: 'purché tu sia felice'.
'Nonostante', meaning even though, is followed by the subjunctive: 'nonostante sia stanco'.
Use the 'imperfetto' ('era') for how things were and the 'passato prossimo' ('abbiamo visto') for the single completed event.
